title: German: Building Sentences
subtitle: Simple German sentences, piece by piece

cards.note: German likes the time before the object: jeden Morgen Kaffee. The verb always sits in second position.
Wohnen means to live somewhere, to reside. Leben means to be alive, though Sie lebt in Berlin works too.

cards.prompt: We are going to Rome tomorrow.
cards.note: German often uses the present tense for the future when a time word is there. Nach is used for cities and most countries.
In yes/no questions the verb comes first. Helfen takes the dative, so it's mir, not mich.
Kein negates nouns, nicht negates verbs and adjectives. So it's keine Zeit, never nicht Zeit.
Nächste means both next and nearest. W-questions put the verb in second place: Wo ist...?

cards.prompt: He has lived here for years.
cards.note: German uses the present tense with seit for something still going on. Seit takes the dative: seit Jahren, seit drei Tagen.
Heute comes before the adjective here: ist heute schön. Wetter is neuter: das Wetter.
Spoken German uses the Perfekt for the past: haben plus participle, and the participle gekauft goes to the end.

cards.prompt: My brother is older than me.
cards.answer: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich
cards.note: Comparisons use -er plus als, and short adjectives often get an umlaut: alt, älter.

cards.prompt: We have to leave at eight.
cards.answer: Wir müssen um acht Uhr gehen
cards.note: With modal verbs like müssen, the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive. Clock times take um: um acht Uhr.
Sprechen changes its vowel: ich spreche, du sprichst, sie spricht. Die Sprache means language.

cards.prompt: The book is on the table.
cards.answer: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch
cards.note: German says whether something lies or stands: liegt for flat things, steht for upright ones. Auf plus dative shows location.
Ausgehen is separable, so aus jumps to the end. Heute Abend means this evening or tonight.
Könntest du is the polite form, just like could you. The infinitive öffnen goes to the end.
Fisch is masculine, so kein becomes keinen in the accusative.
German says the train has lateness: hat Verspätung. Verspätung is a noun, from spät.

cards.prompt: How long does the trip take?
cards.note: Dauern means to last or take time. Die Fahrt is a trip by car, bus or train.
Möchte is the polite way to say what you want, like would like. The infinitive bestellen goes to the end.
Werden plus infinitive forms the future, and the infinitive goes to the end. Because morgen comes first, the verb wird moves before es.
Nicht usually goes to the end of a simple main clause. Dich is the informal you; to a stranger you'd say Ich verstehe Sie nicht.
Das Kind, die Kinder: many neuter nouns form the plural with -er, often with an umlaut.
Anfangen is separable: the prefix an jumps to the end. Fangen also changes its vowel: fängt.
German puts the time word early: bin heute sehr müde. Time before manner before place is a good rule of thumb.
Germans call a mobile phone das Handy. The participle vergessen goes to the end of the sentence.

cards.prompt: I live right by the station.
cards.note: Am is short for an dem. An plus dative describes a place right next to something.
Solltest is the advice form of sollen. The infinitive schlafen goes last.
Mit Karte means by card, bar means in cash. The verb bezahlen goes to the end after the modal kann.
Sich freuen auf is reflexive: ich freue mich. Darauf stands in for auf es, and schon adds a warm already.
Anrufen is separable, but after a modal verb it stays in one piece at the end. It takes the accusative: mich.
